features.title: JR: Faces the Size of Buildings
features.standfirst: How a Paris graffiti writer with a found camera started pasting giant portraits on walls, why the people in the pictures help put them up, and what happened when he took the method to a border, a favela and the Louvre.
features.body:
Stand in front of a JR wall and the first thing you notice is a stranger looking back at you, a face so large that the windows of the building become part of it. There is no frame, no caption and usually no permission slip. Then you notice that the paper is already starting to peel.

A camera on the Métro

JR was born in Paris in 1983 to Eastern European and Tunisian immigrant parents, and started out as a graffiti writer at thirteen under the name Face 3 (Brooklyn Museum). The turn came in 2001, when he found a camera on the Paris Métro (Galleria Continua). He started taking pictures and pasting photocopies of them onto walls around the city. He called these street shows Expo 2 Rue, which the Brooklyn Museum translates as sidewalk galleries (Brooklyn Museum).

He works under his initials, which come from his first name, Jean-René (Wikipedia). He has described himself with a word of his own, photograffeur, half photographer and half graffiti writer, and has also said he is “neither a street artist nor a photographer” (same source).

Paper and paste

The pictures are black and white, blown up and wheatpasted onto buildings, as the Brooklyn Museum puts it, “at a monumental scale usually reserved for advertisements” (Brooklyn Museum). For his first big series, Portrait of a Generation, he photographed young people from the Les Bosquets estate with a 28mm wide-angle lens held close to their faces (The Art Story).

Our reading: the lens is the point. A wide lens pushed into a face looks like a pulled expression, a grimace, a dare. Blown up across a wall, it stops being a portrait taken of someone and starts looking like someone performing for you. The people in the pictures were not victims in a news photo. They chose the face they made.

“I own the largest gallery of the world, the walls of the city!” JR, quoted by the Brooklyn Museum

Where the work goes

The places carry the meaning. Portrait of a Generation came out of the estates around Les Bosquets in Montfermeil, where the 2005 riots followed the deaths of two teenagers, Zyed Benna and Bouna Traoré (Brooklyn Museum; The Art Story). In 2007, for Face 2 Face, JR and his collaborator Marco Berrebi pasted portraits of Israelis and Palestinians side by side in eight cities on both sides of the separation wall (Galleria Continua; Wikipedia). For Women Are Heroes he put women’s portraits on some forty buildings in Rio’s Morro da Providência in 2008, and then took the project to Kenya, India and Cambodia (Brooklyn Museum; Galleria Continua).

The pasting is done with the people in the pictures. JR’s own site says he wants local communities to “take part in the act of artistic creation” (jr-art.net). In 2011 he took that further. He won the TED Prize, worth $100,000, and used it to start Inside Out, which prints and posts back portraits sent in by groups anywhere in the world for them to paste up themselves (Brooklyn Museum).

Permission and illusion

As the projects grew, the illegal paste-up turned into the invited commission. In 2016 the Louvre asked him to make its glass pyramid seem to disappear, and he covered it with a black-and-white anamorphic image, one that only lines up from a single spot, so that from there the pyramid seemed to vanish into the palace behind it (Brooklyn Museum; Wikipedia). In September 2017 he put up a giant photograph of Kikito, a one-year-old boy from Tecate in Mexico, at the US–Mexico border, and a month later held a picnic across the fence on the last day of the installation (Brooklyn Museum).

The latest trick was the biggest. In June 2026 he wrapped the Pont-Neuf in Paris in a 120-metre cave of printed fabric, made in homage to Christo and Jeanne-Claude, who wrapped the same bridge in 1985 (Perrotin; Associated Press). “We’re about to leave something pretty incredible in the middle of Paris,” he told the Associated Press before it opened (AP).

The street and the saleroom

The street pieces are not for sale. They are paid for, his own site says, mainly by selling studio works (jr-art.net). Those turn up at auction. On 18 November 2026 Artcurial in Paris sold a large colour print from Women Are Heroes, shot in Phnom Penh, for €16,032 including fees, which means the hammer fell at the low estimate of €12,000, while a Face 2 Face portrait and a Wrinkles of the City piece in the same sale did not find buyers (Artcurial; Artcurial sale results). Most of his lots, though, are prints, and lithographs from editions of 180 or 250 usually sell for hundreds of pounds rather than thousands (MutualArt; Chiswick Auctions).

None of that changes what happens on the wall. The faces go up, people stop, and the weather takes them down. “The images, like life, are ephemeral,” he has said (The Art Story).

features.title: Ben Eine: The Alphabet on the Shutters
features.standfirst: How a London graffiti writer turned shop shutters into giant letters, what goes into each one, and how a word painting ended up as a gift from Downing Street to the White House.
features.body:
In 2010 Ben Eine took the shop shutters of Middlesex Street, on the edge of the City of London, and painted the alphabet along them, one letter to a shutter, with the shopkeepers’ agreement. The letters became the thing he is known for: big, bright, fairground-style capitals that turn a steel roller door into a sign with no message except its own letter.

From tags to type

Eine was born Benjamin Flynn in London in 1970 (Wikipedia) and grew up in south London. He told the Observer he started writing graffiti at about 14 and had been arrested 15 to 20 times (The Guardian, 2010). He later told the Big Issue that the book Subway Art, by Martha Cooper and Henry Chalfant, set him off, and that graffiti eventually cost him a £7,000 fine and about 180 hours of community service (Big Issue, 2020).

The way out ran through a print studio. He met Banksy at a party at the Dragon Bar near Old Street, and the two set up Pictures on Walls to sell affordable screenprints (Big Issue). Eine became its principal screenprinter, pulling editions for Banksy, David Shrigley and others before he went solo (Interview Magazine, 2013; Ocula). That work matters for what came next. Screenprinting is all about flat colour, clean edges and letters that read at a glance.

How the letters are made

Eine has no training in art or typography, and says so (Interview Magazine). He draws a letter, scans it, prints it out and cuts the stencil by hand with a scalpel rather than using design software or a laser cutter (same source). On the street the shutter itself does some of the work. His letters are usually painted in a solid colour with an offset shadow in a second colour, so they seem to stand off the metal.

Our reading of the photographs on this page: the horizontal slats of a shutter break each letter into stripes, and Eine leans into it, often adding stripes or bands of his own. The look borrows from circus posters and old shop signs, and he has given his lettering styles names such as Shutter, Neon, Tenderloin and New Circus (Wikipedia). In 2012 he released Tenderloin as a free font with the type designer Chank Diesel (same source), and in 2019 he set up OurTypes, a platform for licensing his typography (Creative Boom, 2019).

“Typography guides you around a city without you being aware of it.” Ben Eine, Big Issue, 2020

Words, then sentences

Single letters gave way to words. Eine has painted words such as GREAT ADVENTURE in Beijing, Dallas, San Francisco, Copenhagen and Japan (Interview Magazine). A later wall in Zürich spells out LOVE AT FIRST SIGHT in stacked, striped capitals across the side of a building (photograph below). The words are short and mostly cheerful. The point is the shape of the letters as much as what they say.

The best known canvas is a word piece too. In July 2010 the new prime minister, David Cameron, gave President Obama Eine’s painting Twenty First Century City as an official gift (The Guardian, 22 July 2010). Brooklyn Street Art reported that Samantha Cameron picked the artist (Brooklyn Street Art). The Obamas gave back a signed lithograph by Ed Ruscha, another artist who paints words (The Guardian).

Where it sits now

Eine’s work hangs in the Victoria and Albert Museum’s collection (Ocula), and he was included in Art in the Streets at the Museum of Contemporary Art, Los Angeles, in 2011 (Wikipedia). He uses his name for causes as well. In March 2020 he guest-edited the Big Issue and made the cover for its 200 millionth copy (Big Issue). He accepts that what he paints outside will not last. “Things we paint on the street are painted with the understanding that they’re not going to be there forever,” he told Creative Boom (Creative Boom).

At auction his market is mostly prints. MutualArt lists 172 Eine lots offered in 2025 and 2026, and the recent ones that sold mostly made a few hundred pounds or less, with prices given including buyer’s premium where the auction house says so (MutualArt; Tate Ward).

features.title: Andy Warhol and the Street: The Pop Artist Who Painted with a Graffiti Writer
features.standfirst: Warhol never sprayed a wall, but he spent two years painting with Jean-Michel Basquiat, who began as the downtown graffiti writer SAMO. What the four-handed canvases borrowed from the street.
features.body:
Andy Warhol never wrote on a wall. He worked in a studio, printed his pictures through silkscreens and sold them through galleries. Yet the story of street art in New York keeps running into him, because in the early 1980s the most famous painter in the city spent two years making pictures with a young man who had started out spraying words around downtown Manhattan.

SAMO on the walls

From May 1978, Jean-Michel Basquiat and his school friend Al Diaz wrote short, deadpan phrases signed SAMO© on buildings in SoHo and the East Village, around the School of Visual Arts and on the D train (Wikipedia, SAMO). The Village Voice ran a piece on the mystery writer in December 1978. When the two fell out in early 1980, Basquiat finished the project by writing SAMO© IS DEAD across downtown (same source).

Around the same time he was selling hand-made postcards in SoHo. He is thought to have first met Warhol in 1979, when he tried to sell him some (The Art Newspaper). The real introduction came in October 1982, when the dealer Bruno Bischofberger brought him to lunch at Warhol's studio. Warhol took a Polaroid, and by Warhol's own account a painting came back within two hours, still wet (Wikipedia, Jean-Michel Basquiat).

Four hands, one canvas

The two are thought to have made about 160 works together between 1983 and 1985 (The Art Newspaper). The early pieces began with Warhol's own silkscreened images, eggs, crabs and dollar signs, which Basquiat painted over. Basquiat later put it simply: Warhol would start a painting and he would deface it (e-flux).

That is close to a description of street practice moved indoors. A printed, commercial image goes up first, and a second hand writes over it. Warhol said he thought the paintings were better when you could not tell who had done which part (same source). In our reading, that is the moment the two worlds meet: Pop art's ready-made pictures, and graffiti's habit of answering whatever is already on the wall.

A printed image goes up first, and a second hand writes over it.

A panned show and a long afterlife

The joint exhibition at the Tony Shafrazi Gallery in New York in 1985 did not go well. Critics panned it, one called Basquiat Warhol's mascot, and the friendship cooled (Wikipedia, Jean-Michel Basquiat). Warhol died in February 1987 and Basquiat in August 1988.

Keith Haring, who had known Basquiat from the School of Visual Arts scene (same source), described the collaboration as a conversation held through painting instead of words. When the Fondation Louis Vuitton in Paris showed more than 80 of the jointly signed canvases in 2023, it hung work by Haring and Kenny Scharf beside them (e-flux).

Why it matters on the street

From 1962 Warhol worked by taking a familiar photograph and printing it again and again through a silkscreen (MoMA). In our reading, the stencils, paste-ups and stickers that repeat one picture across a city work in much the same way. His paintings are still on the market this month. Our sister sites, Global Art Monitor and The Art World Report, follow the November 2026 results.

features.title: Konn Artiss: Art, Intervention and Public Attention
features.standfirst: Konn Artiss makes work for the moment a crowd realises something wasn’t supposed to be there. A profile of an artist whose best-known pieces start as public interventions and end up as arguments about who art is for.
features.body:
When people realise that what they’re looking at wasn’t supposed to be there, a crowd goes quiet for a second or two. Then the phones come out. Konn Artiss makes work for that second, and for what happens after it.

For Artiss, as for many artists of this generation, the gallery is one stop in an artwork’s life rather than its starting point. The work usually appears first in public, placed or staged somewhere that already means something, and it borrows the attention of people who weren’t looking for art. Exhibition, collection and auction come later, after the piece has been photographed, discussed and argued over.

Starting outside the white cube

“Street art” covers some of this. The unannounced appearance, the dependence on location and the sense of the city as co-author all come from the street. The strategy owes as much to performance and conceptual art, though. An intervention cares less about how it looks than about what changes when it turns up.

That changes where the viewer stands. You can admire a mural from across the road. An intervention makes you part of its audience whether you meant to be or not, and your reaction (the double take, the photo, the post) becomes part of how the work travels.

Venice as a stage

Venice sharpens all of this. The city is already a spectacle, and every other year it hosts the most closely watched exhibition in contemporary art, so its visitors arrive ready to look. Artiss’s Venice intervention used that readiness. The city provided the drama and the work interrupted it.

Several things make Venice suit this kind of art. Narrow sightlines and routes along the water turn any unexpected object into an event. Nearly every visitor carries a camera. During the Biennale the line between the official programme and unofficial responses to it blurs, and people go looking for the next thing to see. A work placed there gets compared with the pavilions, with the city, and with earlier artists who used Venice the same way. (We cover that history in Venice as a Stage for Contemporary Art.)

The city provided the drama. The work interrupted it.

Attention as a material

Critics of public interventions often call them stunts. The forms can look alike, so the reflex is understandable, but it misses how carefully serious artists in this field work. Artiss handles attention the way other artists handle paint, steel or light.

In practice that means planning for documentation, since most people will see the work on a screen and the photograph will outlive the object. It means thinking about timing and about who will be there, and checking that the piece reads at a glance and still holds up on a second look. It also means treating the public’s response, whether enthusiasm, confusion or irritation, as part of what the work means.

As with any art made in public, the real test comes after the attention moves on. Clever interventions tend to evaporate. The lasting ones leave an idea that people keep coming back to.

From the street to the collection

Every artist who works in public runs into the same practical problem: how does a temporary gesture become something that can be exhibited, bought and kept? Artiss treats the intervention and the collectable work as related but separate. The public piece makes the argument. Studio works, editions and documentation take it into private and institutional collections.

Collectors need to understand that separation. Value here depends on provenance and clarity: knowing exactly what an object is, how it relates to the public work, and who vouches for its authenticity. Gallery representation is one link in that chain. From Public Spectacle to Collectable Object explains how it works.

Why it matters now

Street Art Dispatch exists because this way of working has moved from the edge of contemporary culture to its centre. The artists we follow don’t choose between the street and the gallery. They build practices that move between the two, and they use public space to reach people that institutions rarely reach.

Artiss is a clear example of that shift. The work asks who decides where art can appear, and makes a good case that the people who own the walls no longer decide alone.

features.title: Mohamed L’Ghacham: Family Photographs on the Scale of a Street
features.standfirst: A muralist from Tangier, based near Barcelona, who paints other people’s old snapshots across whole walls. How the pictures are chosen, how they are painted, and five walls from Mallorca to Vienna.
features.body:
Most murals are made to be seen from across a street. Mohamed L’Ghacham’s are made from photographs that were never meant to leave a family album: a birthday cake being cut, children outside a house, neighbours at a table. He paints them across whole walls, in towns across Europe, and the private snapshot becomes something a whole street looks at.

From Tangier to Mataró

L’Ghacham was born in Tangier, Morocco, in 1993 and is based in Mataró, on the coast north of Barcelona (Nuart Aberdeen). He found graffiti at school and only later turned to the classical painters (North West Walls). Among the painters he names as influences are Antonio López and Pere Llobera (Vision Art Festival).

His first murals were not commissions. He told Colossal they were painted in abandoned or demolished places, or simply on the edges of cities (Colossal, 2021).

How the pictures are made

The work is figurative and close to realism, with what festival organisers describe as Impressionist touches (Nuart Aberdeen). The source is almost always a photograph from the late twentieth century. Colossal noted that he looks for photographs with small accidents in them, because they make the scene feel real (Colossal, 2019). The colours are muted and the brushwork is loose and layered (same source).

The photographs come from the places he paints. By 2021 he was working from snapshots and home videos lent by neighbours and from city archives (Colossal, 2021). In Estarreja, Portugal, he used a 1930s photograph of the doctor Egas Moniz with his assistant Deolinda at Santa Marta Hospital in Lisbon, from Moniz’s own archive (mohamedlghacham.com).

Five walls

Casa Paquita, Can Picafort, Mallorca, 2017. Painted for the Saladina Art Fest on one of the oldest houses in the town. The image shows the owner Paquita’s children about forty years earlier, in the same spot, from a photograph she let him use (Street Art United States).

Por Angelo!, Lioni, Italy, 2018. Painted for the Biennale Angelo Garofalo (mohamedlghacham.com). The same year he painted De Fiesta with Alba Trench in Werchter, Belgium, for North West Walls (same source).

La Fondue, Crans-Montana, Switzerland, 2019. Painted for Vision Art Festival, which lists the wall at 1,500 metres (Vision Art Festival).

A birthday cake, Ostend, Belgium. A woman cutting a birthday cake. The city’s art route says he wanted to show the mother as a central figure in the family, and saw the cake as a sign of how things are divided unequally. The work can no longer be seen (The Crystal Ship). The date is to confirm.

the table is set, Vienna, 2025. Listed among Calle Libre’s 2025 walls, in the Meidling district. A family shares a meal while plants grow over the picture, which the festival describes as a fading memory and a small, reachable utopia (Calle Libre).

Private snapshots, painted for a whole street to see.

Off the wall

L’Ghacham also paints at studio scale. He showed with PDP Gallery at the Moniker Art Fair in Brooklyn in May 2018 (mohamedlghacham.com), and Colossal reported a planned solo show of his smaller paintings at PDP Gallery in the summer of 2021 (Colossal, 2021). We have found no public auction result for his work as of November 2026.

features.title: What Makes an Art Intervention Different from a Publicity Stunt?
features.standfirst: Both appear without warning, draw a crowd and spread online. Five questions for telling art made in public apart from marketing made to trend.
features.body:
On paper the two can look identical. Something appears in public without warning, a crowd gathers, photographs spread, and an artist’s or a brand’s name trends for a day. Most of us still sense that an art intervention and a publicity stunt are different things. Saying exactly how is harder.

The shared toolkit

Both rely on surprise, location and circulation. Both need an audience that didn’t plan to be one. Both are now made with the camera in mind, because an event nobody photographs barely happened. That overlap is why critics call artists’ work a stunt so often, and why brands keep borrowing street art’s language.

Five questions that separate them

  1. What’s left once it’s over? A stunt has done its job when attention peaks. An intervention should leave something behind: an idea, an argument, a different way of seeing a place.
  2. Does the site matter? Interventions usually belong to the place where they happen, and moving them drains their meaning. Stunts travel well. The same activation could run in any city with enough footfall.
  3. Who benefits? If the main result is a product launch or more followers, the answer is obvious. Art can raise an artist’s profile too, but the audience should get more out of it than it gives.
  4. Does it survive without the headlines? Look at what was actually made. If it’s still precise and still says something, it will outlast the photograph.
  5. Is the risk real? Artists working in public often take real legal, financial and reputational risks. Stunts are usually permitted, insured and engineered to be safe.

Three cases

During the 2019 Biennale, Banksy set up an unannounced stall in Venice selling paintings that together showed a huge cruise ship dwarfing the city. Police moved the stall on. It looked like a stunt, but the subject belonged to the place: what mass tourism does to the lagoon. The location carried the argument.

Maurizio Cattelan’s Comedian, a banana duct-taped to a wall at Art Basel Miami Beach in 2019, is harder to place. Part of its fame came from another artist eating it. Its subject, though, was how the art market decides what things are worth, so the spectacle was its medium. In 2024 an edition sold at Sotheby’s for $6.2 million, and the argument that followed made Cattelan’s point for him.

Christo and Jeanne-Claude sit at the other end. Wrapping the Reichstag in Berlin in 1995 took more than twenty years of negotiation, and the artists paid for it by selling their own preparatory works. It was slow and expensive, and few public artworks have drawn bigger crowds.

Ask what remains once the noise stops.

A working definition

An art intervention borrows the methods of public spectacle to say something that outlasts the spectacle. A publicity stunt is finished when the spectacle ends. The line isn’t always clean, and the best artists work along it on purpose (our profile of Konn Artiss looks at one). The five questions will usually tell you which side a work falls on.

features.title: Venice as a Stage for Contemporary Art
features.standfirst: A city built as a sequence of reveals, where the art world arrives every other year ready to look. Why Venice is the most loaded stage in public art.
features.body:
Venice has always been staged. A city built on water and laid out as a series of reveals (a bridge, a corner, a sudden campo) teaches visitors to look. That makes it one of the most powerful settings in the world for contemporary art, and one of the most loaded.

A city built for spectators

The Venice Biennale, first held in 1895, made an institution of that theatre. Every other year, national pavilions in the Giardini and the Arsenale bring the art world to one city, and collateral shows fill palazzos, churches and courtyards across the islands. For a few months almost any wall in Venice could be an exhibition space, and almost any visitor a critic.

Official and unofficial Venice

All that attention produces a second, unofficial Biennale. Artists without a pavilion or an invitation know the audience is in town and inclined to read anything unexpected as art. Some of the most discussed works of recent editions appeared on that fringe.

In 2019 Banksy set up an unannounced stall of paintings that together showed a giant cruise ship looming over the city. Around the same time, a mural of a child in a life jacket holding a pink flare appeared at the waterline of a canal-side building. Both dealt with things Venice lives with every day: mass tourism and migration. Neither had the Biennale’s permission, and both relied on its audience.

Sanctioned work has used the city just as boldly. For the 2017 Biennale, Lorenzo Quinn’s Support showed two giant hands rising from the Grand Canal to brace the façade of a historic hotel. The image of a city at risk from climate change spread well beyond the art press.

In Venice the setting always becomes part of the work.

Why interventions land here

Three things make Venice unusually receptive. The first is sightlines: without cars, people walk slowly and look closely. The second is symbolism. Venice already stands for beauty, fragility and overtourism, so any work placed there inherits a metaphor. The third is documentation, since visitors photograph an intervention from every angle within minutes.

The same things make the city hard to work in. A piece that only uses Venice as a backdrop looks thin beside the real thing. The interventions that last, including those by artists such as Konn Artiss, deal with what the city is as well as how it looks.

After the show

Venice also shows how fast public art turns into history. Murals fade in the salt air, temporary works come down, stalls get moved on. Documentation and memory survive, and increasingly so do the collectable objects these moments produce. That’s why our Intervention Archive treats Venice as a core city. A large share of the story of art made in public has happened on its water.

features.title: From Public Spectacle to Collectable Object
features.standfirst: A canvas shreds itself seconds after the hammer falls, then resells for eighteen times the price. How a public spectacle becomes something a collector can own.
features.body:
On 5 October 2018, seconds after the hammer fell on Banksy’s Girl with Balloon at Sotheby’s London, a shredder hidden in the frame started up and pulled half the canvas through. The room gasped. Within days the work had a new title, Love is in the Bin, and was on its way to becoming one of the best-known artworks of the century.

The buyer, who had agreed to pay £1,042,000, went through with the purchase. Three years later the shredded work came back to auction and sold for £18,582,000. The shredding had made the object far more valuable.

The paradox of public art

Art made in public is hard to own. A mural belongs to its wall, and an intervention happens and is gone. Even so, street and urban art has one of the busiest markets in contemporary collecting. It works by translation: the public event is carried into objects that can hold its meaning inside a collection.

What collectors actually buy

  • Studio originals. Unique works on canvas, panel or paper, made for exhibition and sale. They are often the closest link to an artist’s public practice.
  • Editions and prints. Screen prints and other multiples, usually signed and numbered. Shepard Fairey built much of his practice around editions, so for him the print is central.
  • Relics and documentation. Objects, photographs and certificates tied to a specific intervention. Their value depends entirely on clear provenance.
  • Certificates and instructions. Some works exist mainly as an idea. Cattelan’s Comedian is sold as a certificate of authenticity with instructions, and the banana itself can be replaced.

Provenance is everything

Street-based work is easy to imitate, so authentication matters more here than almost anywhere else in contemporary art. Banksy’s works are authenticated by Pest Control, the artist’s own handling service. It refuses to authenticate pieces made on the street, as a stand against people removing public works to sell them. Other artists rely on their galleries, studios and catalogues.

For a new collector the rules are simple. Buy from galleries and auction houses that can document an object’s history. Ask exactly what you’re buying: a unique work, an edition (which number, out of how many) or documentation. Be wary of anything said to have come off a wall.

The shredding made the object worth eighteen times more.

Where the value comes from

The market tends to reward the qualities that make public art matter in the first place: a clear idea, a memorable moment, a recognisable voice. An intervention that really changed the conversation gives every related object a story, and in collecting a story adds value. The best galleries in this field show street-rooted artists alongside the context of their public work.

The shredder’s lesson for collectors is that in this field the artwork and the event are now bound together. The most interesting collections take account of both.

features.title: Banksy and the Evolution of Art Interventions
features.standfirst: Bristol walls, museum hangs, a month-long residency, a theme park and a self-shredding canvas: how one artist turned the intervention from trespass into a global event.
features.body:
No artist has done more to define the modern art intervention than Banksy, and none has changed the form as often. Following the work from Bristol’s walls to the auction room shows how the intervention itself developed, from trespass into a carefully planned public event.

1990s: the wall

The early work came out of Bristol’s graffiti scene in the 1990s. Stencils became the signature, partly because they’re quick to apply and partly because they produce images that read instantly. At this stage the intervention is simple: an image in the wrong place, saying something the wall’s owner never meant to say.

2005: the institution

In 2005 the target moved from the street to the museum. Banksy hung altered works without permission in New York institutions including the Museum of Modern Art and the Metropolitan Museum of Art, and placed a fake “ancient” rock carving of a figure pushing a shopping trolley in the British Museum. Some of these stayed up for days before anyone noticed. The question underneath was who decides what counts as art.

2006–2013: the system

Next the interventions went after systems instead of places. In 2006 hundreds of copies of a Paris Hilton album in UK record shops were swapped for versions the artist had re-sleeved and remixed. In October 2013 the month-long Better Out Than In residency put a new work somewhere in New York every day, and the city became a scavenger hunt played out online. On one day a stall near Central Park sold signed canvases for $60 each, and almost nobody stopped to buy.

2015–2019: the experience

By the mid-2010s the interventions had become places you could walk into. Dismaland (2015), a dystopian “bemusement park” on a derelict lido in Weston-super-Mare, brought together dozens of artists for five weeks. The Walled Off Hotel (2017) in Bethlehem faces the separation wall and runs as both a hotel and an exhibition space. In 2018 the shredding of Girl with Balloon turned an auction room into the stage. In 2019 the Venice stall and mural took on the Biennale, and later that year Gross Domestic Product, a Croydon shop window that never opened, played out a trademark dispute in public.

The surprise stayed constant. The audience grew from one passer-by to the whole internet.

What changed

Surprise runs through all three decades. Scale and planning changed. The early stencils depended on someone happening to notice. The later interventions were built to circulate worldwide: confirmed on the artist’s own channels, documented by the studio, and set up so that the public’s reaction became part of the work.

Banksy wasn’t working alone. Invader’s tile mosaics, appearing in Paris since 1998, and Shepard Fairey’s sticker campaign, started in 1989, built their own systems for occupying the city. All three are in our Intervention Archive.

The legacy for today’s artists

Every artist working in public now, Konn Artiss included, works in a landscape Banksy helped shape. Audiences expect art to appear without warning, the press knows how to cover it, and the market knows how to price what comes out of it. The next generation has to find interventions that can still surprise an audience that has learned to expect surprise.

features.title: How Banksy’s Style Works: Girl with Balloon and Laugh Now
features.standfirst: A stencil, a single colour and a line of dry text. How Banksy builds an image that reads in a second, shown through two of his best-known pictures.
features.body:
Banksy’s pictures are built to be understood in a second. A flat black figure, one line of text or one patch of colour, and a twist that turns the image against whoever is in charge. This piece looks at how that style works, using two well-known images: Girl with Balloon and Laugh Now.

The method: the stencil

A stencil is a sheet with shapes cut out of it. Hold it to a wall, spray paint through it, and the image appears in seconds. Banksy came out of Bristol’s graffiti scene in the 1990s, and the stencil became his signature there (Jordan Schnitzer Museum of Art research guide). The guide describes him as an early mainstream innovator of stencil graffiti.

The same stencil can be used again on a wall, a canvas or a print, which is why one image can exist in many forms. On canvas he often mixes spray paint with acrylic or household emulsion. He also makes screenprint editions and sculptural pieces from found objects.

What you see in the work

“Street art” and “stencil graffiti” are the established labels. What follows is our own description of what the pictures share:

  • Hard edges. Figures are flat silhouettes with crisp outlines, with no shading or brushwork.
  • A small palette. Mostly black and white, often with a single accent colour, frequently red.
  • Familiar characters. Rats, chimpanzees, children, police officers and soldiers stand in for people and power.
  • Short, dry text. When there are words, there are few of them, and they carry the joke.
  • One idea per image. The picture reads at a glance, then the sting follows.

Girl with Balloon

The image first appeared as a stencil on London’s South Bank, near Waterloo Bridge, in 2002 (JSMA guide; Wikipedia). A small girl in black silhouette reaches towards a heart-shaped balloon drifting out of reach. The balloon is the only red in the picture, so the eye goes straight to it.

Most of the picture is empty space between the girl and the balloon, and that gap is the story. Our reading: it can be seen as loss, hope or letting go, and it is left open on purpose. The image was later made as canvases and screenprint editions. In October 2018 a framed version was partly shredded by a device hidden in its frame at Sotheby’s London moments after it sold, and was renamed Love is in the Bin (From Public Spectacle to Collectable Object).

Laugh Now

A stooping chimpanzee wears a sandwich board that reads “Laugh now, but one day we’ll be in charge”. The 2001 canvas, in acrylic and spray paint and 91.5 by 91.5 cm, was described in Bonhams’ catalogue for its October 2026 sale as a dark silhouette cut sharply against a pale green ground (Bonhams lot 9). The same note records that the motif was scaled up in 2002 as a six-metre mural commissioned by the Ocean Rooms nightclub in Brighton.

Here the street method moves onto canvas unchanged: one figure, one flat colour behind it, one line of text. Our reading: the joke flips who is on top. The figure looks submissive, but the words carry a threat.

One figure, one colour, one line. The joke lands first and the point follows.

Why it matters

The style explains much of how the work travels. An image that reads in a second works on a wall, on a phone screen and on a print. For collectors, it also means the same image can appear as a unique canvas or as an edition of hundreds, which is why it always matters to ask exactly which one you are looking at. Every authentic work is certified by Pest Control, the artist’s own authentication body.

features.title: Five Street Artists, Five Styles: From São Paulo to Yogyakarta
features.standfirst: Painted dream worlds, carved faces, X-eyed cartoons, stitched comics and quiet figures. How five street artists from five continents built styles you can recognise from across a street.
features.body:
Street art no longer has one home. The five artists here started on walls in São Paulo, Lisbon, New York, Yogyakarta and South Africa, and each built a style you can recognise from across a street. This piece looks at how each style works, through two pictures per artist.

OSGEMEOS, São Paulo

The twin brothers Gustavo and Otavio Pandolfo started as graffiti artists, and their name means “the twins” in Portuguese (Artsy). Their walls and canvases share one dream world of thin, yellow-skinned figures in patterned clothes.

In 2007 the owners of Kelburn Castle in Scotland asked four Brazilian street artists, OSGEMEOS among them, to paint the outside of the 13th century building (Hyperallergic). The figures and patterns wrap round towers and turrets, treating the whole building as one surface. In the studio the same world becomes objects: Sem medo de ser feliz (2010) is acrylic, spray enamel, latex and sequins on panel (Christie’s). The sequins make the surface glitter, something a wall cannot do.

Vhils, Lisbon

Alexandre Farto works by taking away rather than adding. He cuts, drills, etches or blasts into walls, posters, doors and metal until a face appears (vhils.com). His Scratching the Surface walls were first shown in Lisbon in 2007 and at the Cans Festival in London in 2008 (same source).

The studio works use the same idea on smaller things. Attrition series #01 (2018) is a stack of advertising posters collected from the street and carved by hand, so the colours of old adverts become the light and shade of a face (Bonhams). In our reading, the portraits seem to come out of the city’s own layers.

KAWS, New York

Brian Donnelly tagged “KAWS” on walls in New Jersey and Manhattan, then began painting his own cartoon figures onto bus shelter adverts (Christie’s guide). The figures have X’s for eyes, and the main character, COMPANION, first appeared as a toy in 1999 (same source).

The toy grew into sculpture: COMPANION (ORIGINALFAKE) (2011) is fibreglass and paint, almost two and a half metres tall (Christie’s). The paintings crop the cartoons tight. CAMO CAN’T HELP YOU (2013) breaks its figures into flat zones of colour with crisp edges across a canvas three metres wide (Christie’s).

Eko Nugroho, Yogyakarta

Eko Nugroho makes murals, paintings, embroidery and sculpture, often with local communities (Singapore Art Museum). His figures come from comics and are usually masked; the museum says he avoids stereotyped faces on purpose (same source).

His embroidered picture Illusion (2007), now at the Singapore Art Museum, shows a stripped landscape with monster-like machines and a masked figure (same source). Trap Costum for President 1 (2011) uses the same stitched comic style for a joke about power (Christie’s). Moving a wall image into thread keeps it flat and bright.

Faith XLVII, South Africa

Faith XLVII began writing graffiti on South African streets in 1997 as Faith47, and has since painted public murals in 39 countries (Strauss & Co). Her figures are calm and almost religious, often with a Latin or Afrikaans phrase.

Her 2014 mural Capax Infiniti on the Carlyle building in Portland, Oregon, later became a lithograph with the same title (Strauss & Co). The triptych Coltan; Oil; Diamonds, mixed media on panel in frames she made by hand, names three resources mined in Africa (Strauss & Co). In our reading, the three panel altarpiece shape joins her spiritual style to a political subject.

Five cities, five methods: paint, carving, cartoons, thread and quiet figures.

What they share

Each artist kept the street’s need to be read at a glance, then found a studio form that adds something a wall cannot: sequins, carved paper, fibreglass, embroidery or a hand-made frame. Recent auction results for all five are on our sister site, Global Art Monitor.

features.title: Why Contemporary Artists Are Working Beyond Gallery Walls
features.standfirst: The white cube was designed to remove distractions, and many artists now find that neutrality limiting. Five reasons the work is moving outside.
features.body:
The white cube was designed to remove distractions: clean walls, even light, nothing between the viewer and the work. A growing number of contemporary artists now find that neutrality limiting. They’re taking work into streets, squares and waterways and onto screens, and their reasons go well beyond rebellion.

1. The audience is elsewhere

Most people never visit a contemporary gallery. Public space reaches commuters, residents, tourists and children. Keith Haring understood this in the early 1980s, when he drew in chalk on the black paper covering unused advertising panels in the New York subway and made work for thousands of riders a day.

2. Context is content

A work placed somewhere specific takes on that place’s history and politics. JR’s huge paste-ups get their meaning from where they go up, from the portraits in Women Are Heroes to the 2016 illusion that made the Louvre pyramid seem to vanish.

3. Documentation travels further than objects

A gallery show reaches the people who visit. A public work that gets photographed and shared can reach millions within hours. The image of an intervention now counts as a work in its own right, and it’s often how most people experience it.

4. Participation changes the work

Public art lets people in. JR’s Inside Out project, launched in 2011, asks communities around the world to paste up their own portraits. Invader’s Flash Invaders app turns finding the mosaics into a game played across cities. The audience takes part as well as looking.

5. The gallery still matters, differently

The gallery isn’t finished. Its role is shifting from the place where art starts to the place where it’s gathered, explained and kept. Galleries working with street-rooted artists show studio works, editions and documentation that carry a public practice into collections.

The work starts in the street. The gallery keeps the story.

The risks

Working outside the gallery has costs. Unsanctioned work can bring legal trouble, temporary work can disappear without a record, and public attention moves on quickly. Careful, searchable, accurate documentation matters for exactly that reason, and it’s why Street Art Dispatch is building an archive of public interventions.

columns.title: The Phone Is the New Plinth
columns.standfirst: Every public artwork now lives twice, once on the street and once on the screen. Most of its audience only ever sees the screen.
columns.body:
Every public artwork now has two lives, one on the street and one on the screen. For most of its audience the screen is the only one they see.

Artists working in public have adapted quickly. They compose works to read in a vertical frame, time them for when feeds are busiest, and release their own documentation so that the first image to circulate is the right one. Social platforms did for urban art what the printing press did for the poster, making the image endlessly reproducible and putting it in everyone’s pocket.

That brings opportunity and pressure. An artist with a strong online following can work without institutions. The platforms reward novelty over depth, though, and it’s tempting to make work for the scroll instead of the street.

The most interesting artists use the phone the way a sculptor uses a plinth: to present the work, which still lives somewhere else.

columns.title: Anatomy of a Viral Artwork
columns.standfirst: What makes a work of public art travel? The same four ingredients keep turning up, and quality isn’t one of them.
columns.body:
What makes a work of public art travel? Across the most-shared interventions of the past decade, the same ingredients keep turning up.

  1. A readable image. The work makes sense in under a second, even as a thumbnail.
  2. A recognisable setting. A famous building, a symbolic city or a familiar street.
  3. A story. Something happened, such as a removal, an arrest, a sale or a disappearance, that gives people a reason to share it.
  4. An open question. Who made it? Is it real? Is it allowed?

Going viral says nothing about quality, and plenty of strong work never travels. Knowing the mechanics helps audiences and editors tell work built to last from work built to trend. For the longer argument, read What Makes an Art Intervention Different from a Publicity Stunt?

columns.title: When the Crowd Becomes the Medium
columns.standfirst: Some interventions aren’t objects. They’re situations, and the public is the material.
columns.body:
Some interventions aren’t objects at all. They’re situations, and the crowd is the material.

Think of the queue outside a shop that never opens, the people gathered around a work that might be removed at any moment, or the hunt across a city for the next piece. In each case, part of the artwork is what the public does.

That puts public art close to performance, in a line that runs back to the happenings of the 1960s. It also raises a question of responsibility. When a crowd becomes the medium, the artist is shaping how people behave in public space as well as what it looks like.

The best work uses that power carefully and gives people something worth discovering.

artists.name: Konn Artiss
artists.summary: An artist working across public intervention, installation and collectable work. Our readers know Artiss best for an intervention staged in Venice that made the city’s audience part of the piece.

artists.name: Banksy
artists.summary: The anonymous artist from Bristol’s graffiti scene who made the stencil a global language and turned interventions into events, from unsanctioned museum hangs to a canvas that shredded itself at auction.
facts: Hand-cut stencils, spray paint, screenprint editions
artists.story:
Nobody has confirmed who Banksy is, and we do not guess. The documented story starts in Bristol, where he was a teenage graffiti writer in the 1990s before moving to London, according to the Jordan Schnitzer Museum of Art. Phillips dates his first works on trains and walls to 1993.

The walls came first, but canvases followed early. Laugh Now, a canvas of 2001, was bought from the artist the year it was painted (Bonhams). In 2006 the Los Angeles show Barely Legal put large paintings such as Angel in front of an American audience (Bonhams).

In the summer of 2009 he took over the museum in his home city. Banksy Versus Bristol Museum filled the building with about 100 works, was free to enter and ran until 31 August. Staff had kept the plan secret since the previous October (Mail & Guardian).
artists.method:
A stencil is a sheet with shapes cut out of it. Hold it to a wall, spray through it, and the picture appears in seconds. The Jordan Schnitzer Museum of Art calls Banksy an early mainstream innovator of stencil graffiti, a technique prized for its speed and graphic clarity. On canvas he mixes spray paint with acrylic or household emulsion (Bonhams).

The look hardly changes between wall and canvas: flat black and white figures, a single accent colour and very few words. Rats and chimpanzees stand in for people. Bonhams’ catalogue for Laugh Now reads the chimpanzee as a stand-in through which human hierarchies are seen (Bonhams).

works.m: Acrylic and spray paint on canvas
works.note: A stooping chimpanzee wears a sandwich board. The image also became a six-metre mural commissioned for the Ocean Rooms nightclub in Brighton in 2002 (Bonhams). Our reading: the joke lands first, and the point about who does the work and who gets laughed at follows a second later.

works.m: Stencil mural, later canvases and prints
works.note: First painted near Waterloo Bridge on London’s South Bank (Wikipedia). A framed version partly shredded itself moments after selling at Sotheby’s in 2018 and was renamed Love Is in the Bin. Offered again in 2021, it sold for £18.6m with fees (The Art Newspaper).

works.m: Reclaimed airport customs arch, wood, metal and spray paint
works.note: A found object, reworked and given a new title. It shows how far the practice has moved from the wall to the gallery (Phillips).

quotes.q: “This is the first show I’ve ever done where taxpayers’ money is being used to hang my pictures up rather than scrape them off.”
quotes.who: Banksy, before Banksy Versus Bristol Museum opened in June 2009, as reported by the Mail & Guardian

A framed Girl with Balloon partly shreds at Sotheby’s

artists.name: Invader
artists.summary: The French artist whose ceramic-tile mosaics, built from the pixel language of early video games, have been “invading” cities since 1998. In 2015 one reached the International Space Station.
artists.story:
Invader is French and keeps his face out of photographs. The Talks gives his year of birth as 1969. He has said the idea for the first wall mosaic came to him at the end of 1996, and that it was only in 1998 that he understood what the gesture could become (Artnet News). Paris was the first city to be ‘invaded’.

By 2022 the count stood at more than 4,000 street works in around 80 cities. One mosaic went to the International Space Station in 2015 with the astronaut Samantha Cristoforetti, and the 4,000th was fixed to a wall in Potosí, Bolivia, at 4,000 metres (Artnet News).

Nearly all of it is unauthorised. He told The Talks that 99 per cent of his pieces are illegal, and he calls museum and city commissions, such as a hospital facade in Paris and a bridge on the Vienna underground, his ‘1 percent legal’ (Artnet News). Theft follows the work. Around 15 pieces were prised off Paris buildings in 2017 by thieves posing as city workers, and he now makes tiles that break if anyone tries to remove them (Artnet News).
artists.method:
The figures come from the 8-bit video games of the 1980s. Each square of a pixel image becomes a ceramic tile, so a mosaic is built the same way an old screen built a picture (Juxtapoz). His early designs were drawn on a Macintosh IIfx with Photoshop 2.0, by his own account.

He also builds pictures from Rubik’s Cubes, which he calls Rubikcubism. Invader Rubikcubist, a show of more than 100 such works, ran at MIMA in Brussels until January 2023 (Artnet News). Our reading: the cube does the same job as the tile, one coloured square at a time.

works.note: Taken aboard the International Space Station by Samantha Cristoforetti, which put an invasion beyond any city (Artnet News).

Installed at an altitude of 4,000 metres to mark the 4,000th piece. The milestone was celebrated with Invader 4,000 at Over the Influence in Paris, from 10 December 2022 to 22 January 2023 (Artnet News).
More than a hundred original works from January to 3 September 2017 (Juxtapoz).

quotes.q: “I hope forever. Because that is the game. I am addicted to it.”
quotes.who: Invader, asked how long the invasions will go on, The Talks

quotes.q: “Invading a new city is always more exciting for me than working on a new show.”

milestones: Idea for the first wall mosaic
The Paris invasion begins in earnest
A mosaic goes to the International Space Station
Hello My Game Is..., Musée en Herbe, Paris
About 15 Paris pieces stolen by fake city workers

Artnet News, Anna Sansom, Invader on installing more than 4,000 mosaics (12 December 2022)

artists.name: Shepard Fairey
artists.summary: The American artist who grew a 1989 student sticker campaign into the OBEY project. His 2008 Hope poster became one of the defining political images of its era.
artists.story:
Shepard Fairey began the campaign that made his name in 1989, as a 19-year-old illustration student at the Rhode Island School of Design in Providence (Los Angeles magazine). It was a sticker of the wrestler André the Giant with the line ‘Andre the Giant Has a Posse’. Fairey has said it ‘started as an inside joke with some skateboard friends’. RISD says it soon turned into a wider statement about making art for everyone (RISD).

The word OBEY came from John Carpenter’s 1988 film They Live. Fairey told RISD students that the word ‘hit me like a ton of bricks’ (RISD). He co-founded the gallery Subliminal Projects in 1995, launched the OBEY clothing label in 2001 and set up the design studio Studio Number One in 2003 (The Creative Independent). He has lived in Los Angeles since 2001.

His Hope portrait of Barack Obama, made during the 2008 election, carried his work far beyond the street. The original is in the Smithsonian (Los Angeles magazine), and his work is also held by MoMA, LACMA and the National Portrait Gallery in Washington (The Creative Independent). The street work never stopped, and it has brought legal trouble, including 14 felony charges for destruction of property in Boston in 2009 (Los Angeles magazine).
artists.method:
Fairey works like a graphic designer: bold shapes, a small set of colours and lettering that reads from across a road. The same image can appear as a sticker, a pasted poster, a mural or a signed screen print. Our reading: the style borrows the look of propaganda in order to make people question it.

Collectors mostly buy his signed screen-print editions, which are produced in numbers. Murals are the public face of the work. By 2019 he had painted 100 of them, the hundredth for the arts organisation AS220 in Providence (RISD).

works.t: Andre the Giant Has a Posse
works.note: Started at RISD and spread by hand, city by city. It is the seed of everything that came later, including the OBEY name (RISD).
Made during the presidential campaign. The original is in the collection of the Smithsonian (Los Angeles magazine).

works.t: Facing the Giant: Three Decades of Dissent
works.note: Shown in Providence at AS220’s gallery from 25 October to 16 November 2019 (RISD), and in Los Angeles at Over the Influence with 30 original works (Los Angeles magazine).

quotes.q: “If you work hard and believe in what you’re doing, the art world will eventually come to you.”
quotes.who: Shepard Fairey, speaking to RISD students in October 2019, RISD

milestones: OBEY clothing; moves to Los Angeles
Charged in Boston over street work
sources: RISD, Fairey Faces the Giant, Simone Solondz (24 October 2019)
Los Angeles magazine, Robert Ito, Shepard Fairey looks back at 30 years of dissent (6 November 2019)

artists.name: OSGEMEOS
artists.summary: Twin brothers from São Paulo who started as graffiti artists and built one dream world of thin, yellow-skinned figures, painted on walls, canvases and once on a Scottish castle.
facts: Spray paint, acrylic, sequins, found doors
artists.story:
OSGEMEOS means ‘the twins’ in Portuguese. Gustavo and Otavio Pandolfo were born in São Paulo in 1974 (NPR) and grew up in Cambuci, an old working-class immigrant neighbourhood of the city (Juxtapoz). Tate’s press release says they started painting graffiti in 1987 (Tate).

As children they invented an imaginary place they call Tritrez (NPR). Our reading: much of what they paint looks like news from that place. They talk about the partnership as a single voice, and work as one.

The walls led quickly to museums. They painted a giant about 82 feet high for the 2004 Athens Olympics (NPR), helped paint Kelburn Castle in Scotland in 2007 (Hookedblog) and in 2008 were among six artists who painted the river front of Tate Modern (Tate). Segredos, their homecoming show at the Pinacoteca de São Paulo, gathered more than 1,000 items, including notebooks from their early teens shown for the first time (Juxtapoz). The Hirshhorn in Washington gave them Endless Story, their first major museum survey in the United States, in 2024 (Jordan Schnitzer Museum of Art).
artists.method:
The figures are long-limbed and yellow-skinned, in patterned clothes, set in dreamlike scenes. Artsy links the imagery to Brazilian folklore, hip-hop and graffiti. A museum research guide says the yellow comes from a colour both brothers see in their dreams (Jordan Schnitzer Museum of Art).

In the studio the paintings grow extra layers. One panel of 2010 combines acrylic, spray enamel, latex and sequins (Christie’s). Others are made on MDF with sequins and found materials, and some move: Untitled (Zoetrope) of 2014 is built around an early animation device (NPR).

works.m: Paint on the walls of a 13th century castle, Scotland
works.note: Commissioned by the castle’s owners from four Brazilian artists, OSGEMEOS among them (Hookedblog). Our reading: a rare case of a historic building choosing graffiti.

works.m: Acrylic, spray enamel, latex and sequins on panel
works.note: The title means ‘without fear of being happy’. The sequins catch the light as you move, so the picture changes as you walk past (Christie’s).
Their largest show in the United States, with more than 1,000 artworks, curated by Marina Isgro and opening on 29 September 2024 (NPR).

quotes.q: “There is a conversation in the air flying there, but only we can listen [to] each other.”

milestones: Start painting graffiti in São Paulo
Giant figure for the Athens Olympics
Tate Modern river front; Museum of Contemporary Art Tokyo
Art in the Streets, MOCA Los Angeles
First US solo show, ICA Boston
When the leaves turn to yellow, CAC Málaga

artists.name: Vhils
artists.summary: The Lisbon artist Alexandre Farto, who makes portraits by cutting, drilling and blasting into walls, posters, doors and metal rather than adding paint.
artists.story:
Alexandre Farto was born in Lisbon in 1987 (vhils.com). He started as an illegal graffiti writer at 13, and by 16 or 17 he had begun to question what he was doing (designboom). At about 19 he went to London to study, at Byam Shaw School of Art and Central Saint Martins (Euronews; vhils.com). In 2008 he painted at the Cans Festival in London, alongside Banksy (Euronews).

The turning point was a change in direction rather than in style. He painted billboards white and cut back through them. ‘I felt that by destroying I was revealing,’ he told designboom (designboom). His studio was founded in 2010 (vhils.com) and now works from Barreiro, on the outskirts of Lisbon, with a team of about 15 (Hypebeast).

Lisbon has given him two museum shows: Prisma, a video installation at MAAT in 2022 (MAAT), and a look back at his printed editions at MUDE, the city’s design museum, in early 2026 (Euronews).
artists.method:
Vhils works by taking away. He cuts, drills, etches or blasts through plaster, paper, wood and metal until a face appears from the layers underneath (vhils.com). The tools run from chisels and a Dremel to explosives, a method he developed around 2012 (Hypebeast).

In the studio he carves into stacks of posters collected from the street, so the colours of old adverts become the light and shade of a portrait (Bonhams). The faces are often of people who live where the wall stands. In Rio de Janeiro he carved portraits into the ruins of homes being demolished, working with a local organisation (Euronews).

works.note: The series that set out the method, first shown in Lisbon in 2007 and in London in 2008 (vhils.com).
A series cut into the bodies of old train carriages (Hypebeast).

works.m: Hand-carved advertising posters collected from the street
works.note: A studio work, 180 by 120 cm. Our reading: the adverts that once sold things now make up a stranger’s face (Bonhams).

quotes.q: “I say that I’m kind of an urban archaeologist because I basically carve on the walls of the city.”
“All of the layers in my work were a part of someone’s life before.”

sources: designboom, Hollie Smith, Alexandre Farto aka Vhils studio visit and interview in Lisbon (19 May 2017)
Euronews, Charlotte Cullen, Meet Vhils, Portugal’s ‘urban archaeologist’ (14 April 2022, updated 14 May 2024)
Hypebeast, Kevin Wong, Exploding Identity with Vhils (9 March 2020)
Euronews, Inês dos Santos Cardoso, Vhils in view (25 January 2026)

artists.name: KAWS
artists.summary: The American artist Brian Donnelly, who began by painting cartoon figures onto bus shelter adverts and turned his X-eyed character COMPANION into toys, paintings and giant sculptures.
facts: Flat colour, cartoon figures, X-ed out eyes
artists.story:
Brian Donnelly was born in 1974. He studied illustration at the School of Visual Arts in New York and painted backgrounds for television cartoons (Christie’s). At night he tagged KAWS on walls in New Jersey and Manhattan, then began opening bus shelter advertising cases, painting his own figures over the posters and putting them back (Christie’s). Untitled (Haring), painted on an advertising poster in 1997, and Untitled (Maidenform) of 1999 date from those years (The Brooklyn Rail; The Art Newspaper).

A trip to Japan in 1999 produced his first toy, COMPANION, a figure with crossed-out eyes (Christie’s). The character has since been carved, cast and inflated. A COMPANION balloon joined the Macy’s Thanksgiving parade in 2012, and a 121-foot inflatable lay in Hong Kong’s Victoria Harbour in 2019 (Christie’s; The Brooklyn Rail). In 2021 the Brooklyn Museum gave him KAWS: WHAT PARTY, his first museum show in New York, with more than 100 works (Brooklyn Museum).
artists.method:
KAWS borrows from cartoons and packaging: flat colour, hard edges and familiar characters with X’d-out eyes. The large paintings crop the figures so tightly that they break into blocks of colour (Christie’s). He keeps the sculptures still on purpose. ‘I want you to look at the form. I don’t want you to think about what they might say,’ he told the Brooklyn Rail (The Brooklyn Rail).

The output is unusually wide: unique paintings, large sculptures, prints, toys, and collaborations with brands including Nike, Uniqlo and Dior (The Art Newspaper). Our reading: that range is what keeps him in the street-art conversation long after he left the bus shelters.

works.m: Acrylic on an existing advertising poster
works.note: One of the altered adverts that started it all, first shown at a friend’s restaurant and gallery in Seattle (The Brooklyn Rail).
The figure with Xs for eyes, first made as a toy after a trip to Japan (Christie’s). It has since appeared at every scale, from a shelf figure to a harbour.
First shown at Kaikai Kiki Gallery in Tokyo. A cartoon face cropped and broken into flat camouflage-like shapes (Christie’s).

quotes.q: “I think no matter what I put on canvas, people don’t think of me as a painter.”

milestones: ORIGINALFAKE COMPANION for his Tokyo shop
CAC Málaga, his first sculpture-only show
sources: Christie’s, 10 things to know about KAWS (28 March 2026)
The Brooklyn Rail, KAWS with Jason Rosenfeld (June 2021)
The Art Newspaper, Paddy Johnson, The Big Review: Kaws at the Brooklyn Museum (9 April 2021)

artists.name: Eko Nugroho
artists.summary: The Yogyakarta artist whose masked, comic-book figures move from walls into paintings, embroidery and batik, often made with local communities.
artists.story:
Eko Nugroho was born in 1977 and lives and works in Yogyakarta, Indonesia (DANYSZ; Singapore Art Museum). He was 20 when President Suharto’s government fell in 1998 after 32 years (DANYSZ). He studied at the Indonesian Institute of the Arts in Yogyakarta, graduating in 2006, and once worked as a primary school teacher (The Jakarta Post).

He started with comics. In 2000, still a student, he founded Daging Tumbuh, a comic magazine whose first issue came out in June that year, and he was part of the Apotik Komik group in Yogyakarta (Art + Australia). His first solo show, Bercerobong (Like a Chimney), was at Cemeti Art House in 2002 (The Jakarta Post).

Museums followed: the Asia Pacific Triennial in Brisbane in 2006, a solo show at the Musée d’Art Moderne de Paris in 2012 and the Indonesian Pavilion at the Venice Biennale in 2013 (Art + Australia). In 2013 he also designed scarves for Louis Vuitton. Only 500 were made (The Jakarta Post).
artists.method:
His figures are masked or hooded, sometimes with extra limbs, and often carry slogans in English or Indonesian. The masks are a choice. ‘I don’t want to pass judgment on somebody,’ he told The Jakarta Post (The Jakarta Post). The Singapore Art Museum says he avoids stereotyped faces that could lead to discrimination (Singapore Art Museum).

The same drawing style moves between murals, paintings and large embroideries. Finding tailors who could stitch what he wanted was hard at first (Art + Australia). Before painting a mural he studies the place it will be in. Since 2008 he has also made performances with the puppet company Wayang Bocor (The Jakarta Post).

works.note: In the Singapore Art Museum: a stripped landscape with monster-like machines and a masked figure (Singapore Art Museum).
A painting whose title, like many of his, reads as a sideways comment on politics (Art + Australia). That reading is ours.
A room-sized work shown around the time of his Paris and Melbourne exhibitions (Art + Australia).

artists.name: Faith XLVII
artists.summary: The South African artist who began writing graffiti as Faith47 in 1997 and has since painted public murals in 39 countries, with calm, almost religious figures.
artists.story:
Faith XLVII was born in 1979 and began writing graffiti as Faith47 on South African streets in 1997 (Strauss & Co). She was born in Cape Town and sprayed her first wall at the old Clovelly train station, with the graffiti writer Wealz130 beside her (Daily Maverick). Through the late 1990s and early 2000s she was one of the most prolific names on the South African scene (Daily Maverick).

From 2006 she travelled to paint murals, and by Strauss & Co’s count she has painted them in 39 countries (Strauss & Co). By 2020 she had been based in Los Angeles for three years (Daily Maverick). Her work has been shown at the Calais Museum of Fine Art, the Bernard Magrez Foundation and the Brooklyn Museum (Strauss & Co), and in 2025 the STRAAT Museum in Amsterdam gave her a show and added a work to its collection (Artdaily).
artists.method:
Her murals are often animals or quiet figures set beside old phrases: a zebra in central Johannesburg, horses on a Los Angeles facade, swans on a Brooklyn rooftop (Daily Maverick). Lettering still matters to her. ‘Fonts, alphabets, this is the stuff of human evolution, of consciousness and articulation,’ she told Daily Maverick.

Away from walls she makes new media installations, hand-sewn hangings, bronzes, paintings and prints (Strauss & Co). The studio work of 2020, made for CHANT at the Everard Read gallery in Cape Town, used flags: white flags in The Unbound and redrawn national flags in Entanglement (Daily Maverick).

works.note: The Latin phrase means ‘holding the infinite’. The wall was later turned into a lithograph with the same title (Strauss & Co).
Painted with the City of Philadelphia Mural Arts Program (Daily Maverick).
National flags drawn by hand, taken apart and overlaid with a circular symbol. The show itself was postponed by lockdown (Daily Maverick).

quotes.q: “These are not works made to be pretty or decorative; these are works made to consider, to dismantle, to question.”
“One can’t stop the clouds from moving. Nothing is permanent.”

artists.name: Mohamed L’Ghacham
artists.summary: A painter and muralist from Tangier, based in Mataró, who turns old family photographs into wall-sized paintings for festivals across Europe.
facts: Murals painted from late 20th century photographs
artists.story:
Mohamed L’Ghacham was born in Tangier in 1993. A few months later his parents moved to Spain, and he grew up in Mataró, outside Barcelona (Juxtapoz). He started painting graffiti with school friends and began painting in the street in earnest in 2008, the year factories in the town closed in the financial crisis (Juxtapoz).

Classical painting pulled him in the other direction. He names Antonio López and Pere Llobera among his influences, alongside muralists such as Axel Void and Aryz (Street Art United States). His first murals were painted in abandoned or demolished places and on the edges of towns (Colossal). Festival walls followed in Mallorca, Belgium, Switzerland, Scotland and Austria.
artists.method:
He paints from real photographs, usually family snapshots from the late 20th century. ‘I almost never depict acted scenes with people posing,’ he told Street Art United States (Street Art United States). Many walls show the families or towns where they are painted, so the picture belonged to someone who can still walk past it.

A wall is a race. ‘When I’m on a wall it’s a fight against the clock,’ he told Juxtapoz, comparing it with the slower pace of the studio (Juxtapoz). Our reading: the loose, quick brushwork that deadline forces on him suits the subject, because memory is blurry too.

works.note: Painted for Saladina Art Fest from a photograph of the owner’s children taken about forty years earlier in the same place (Street Art United States).
A village pig slaughter from an old photograph, an everyday ritual painted at the scale of a building (Colossal).
Painted for Calle Libre in the Meidling district: a family meal, partly overgrown with plants (Calle Libre).

quotes.q: “My paintings usually represent moments of calm and reunion.”
“Until now my intention was to pay tribute and give visibility to situations that we all live in.”

artists.name: Ben Eine
artists.summary: The London artist who paints giant circus-style capitals on shop shutters. He painted the whole alphabet along Middlesex Street, and in 2010 one of his canvases went from Downing Street to the White House.
facts: Spray paint and hand-cut stencils, screenprints
Middlesex Street alphabet (2010) · Twenty First Century City (2010)
artists.story:
Ben Eine grew up in south London and started writing graffiti at about 14. By his own count to the Observer he was arrested 15 to 20 times (The Guardian, 2010). He has said a £7,000 fine and around 180 hours of community service were part of what pushed him from graffiti towards street art (Big Issue, 2020).

He met Banksy at a party at the Dragon Bar near Old Street, and together they started Pictures on Walls to sell cheap screenprints (Big Issue). Eine ran the printing, making editions for Banksy and David Shrigley among others (Interview Magazine, 2013). His own letters went up on shutters around east London, and in 2010 he painted A to Z on the shutters of Middlesex Street, known since as Alphabet Street (Wikipedia).

That July, David Cameron gave Barack Obama Eine’s canvas Twenty First Century City as an official gift (The Guardian). The Victoria and Albert Museum holds his work (Ocula).
artists.method:
Each letter starts as a drawing. Eine scans it, prints it and cuts the stencil with a scalpel, and says he prefers that to drawing on a computer or using a laser cutter (Interview Magazine). The letters are fat display capitals in strong colour with an offset shadow, close to old circus and fairground lettering.

Our reading: the shutter is part of the design. Its slats cut every letter into bands, and he often adds stripes so the pattern looks deliberate. He has named his letter styles, among them Shutter, Neon, Tenderloin and New Circus, and released Tenderloin as a free font in 2012 (Wikipedia).

works.m: Spray paint on shop shutters, London
works.note: All 26 letters, one to a shutter, painted with the shopkeepers’ agreement (Big Issue; Street Art London).

A whole end wall of stacked, striped capitals. Photographed in August 2023 (Wikimedia Commons).

quotes.q: “Typography guides you around a city without you being aware of it.”
“Spraypainting a shop shutter turns an ugly, boring thing into something interesting and colourful.”

artists.name: JR
artists.summary: The Paris artist who prints black-and-white faces at the size of buildings and pastes them up with the people in them. He calls himself a photograffeur, and since 2011 he has handed his method to anyone who wants it through the Inside Out Project.
facts: Large-format photographs, paper and wheat paste, printed fabric
Face 2 Face (2007) · Inside Out (2011) · La Caverne du Pont-Neuf (2026)
artists.story:
JR grew up the child of immigrant parents, one Eastern European and one Tunisian, and was writing graffiti by thirteen (Brooklyn Museum). A camera he found on the Paris Métro in 2001 turned him into a photographer (Galleria Continua), though he kept the graffiti writer’s habits. His pictures went straight onto walls, sometimes illegally (same source).

His first large project, Portrait of a Generation (2004 to 2006), was made with Ladj Ly and showed young people from the Les Bosquets estate in Montfermeil and La Forestière in Clichy-sous-Bois. Riots broke out there in 2005 after two local teenagers died (Brooklyn Museum; The Art Story). Face 2 Face followed in Israel and Palestine, then Women Are Heroes in Rio, Kenya, India and Cambodia (same source). The TED Prize in 2011 paid for Inside Out, a project that prints portraits for other people to paste up (Brooklyn Museum).

His film Faces Places, made with Agnès Varda, won the Golden Eye for documentary at Cannes in 2017 and was nominated for an Oscar (Wikipedia). He is represented by Perrotin, Pace, Galleria Continua, Galeria Nara Roesler and Simon Studer Art (jr-art.net).
artists.method:
The basic kit has hardly changed: a camera, a large-format printer, paper and paste. The portraits are black and white, pasted by hand, often with the help of the people pictured, at the scale of a billboard (Brooklyn Museum; jr-art.net). For his early series he used a 28mm wide-angle lens close to the face (The Art Story).

Our reading: nothing frames the faces, so the building does. Windows become eyes, a roofline becomes a forehead, and the wall’s cracks show through the paper. Since 2016 he has also used anamorphosis, images that only line up from one point, as on the Louvre pyramid (Wikipedia). The paper is meant to fail. Rain and sun wear the pictures away, and he treats that as part of the work.

works.note: Portraits of Israelis and Palestinians pasted side by side in eight cities on both sides of the separation wall (Galleria Continua).

artists.name: Keith Haring
artists.summary: The American artist who drew in white chalk on empty advertising panels in the New York subway, then carried the same bold outline onto public murals from Manhattan to Pisa.
facts: Chalk, then paint; one continuous outline
artists.story:
Keith Haring was born in Reading, Pennsylvania, in 1958 (Britannica) and grew up in Kutztown. He had his first solo show in Pittsburgh at 19, and in 1978 moved to New York to study at the School of Visual Arts, where he fell in with the crowd at Club 57 (PBS American Masters).

In 1981 he started drawing in the subway. Unused advertising panels were covered with black paper until a new poster went up, and Haring drew on them in white chalk, without permission (Britannica). PBS puts the number of these drawings in the hundreds, made over five years (PBS American Masters). Gallery shows followed, at Tony Shafrazi in 1982, and he was in the Whitney Biennial in 1983 (PBS American Masters). He died in New York in 1990, aged 31 (Britannica).
artists.method:
A subway drawing had to be quick, because it was made in a public station by someone who was not meant to be there. The figures are drawn in one continuous outline, with short strokes around them for movement or noise, and the same shapes run through his murals, paintings and prints (Jordan Schnitzer Museum of Art).

Our reading: the speed of the subway work is why the style is so easy to recognise. With no time for shading or detail, everything rests on the outline.

works.m: Chalk on three joined sheets of black paper, on the original transit authority mount
works.note: One of the largest subway drawings of its time, according to the Jordan Schnitzer Museum of Art, with figures tumbling from a body that stands for the year 1985 (JSMA).
Painted in the same year he opened the Pop Shop and painted on the Berlin Wall (PBS American Masters).
Painted on the wall of the Servi di Maria convent beside the church of Sant'Antonio, between the railway and bus stations. The city describes its subject as universal peace (Pisa tourism office).

artists.name: Jean-Michel Basquiat
artists.summary: The Brooklyn-born painter who began as one of the writers behind the SAMO© tags in downtown Manhattan and brought the words, crowns and crossings out of the street onto canvas.
facts: Oilstick, acrylic, words and found materials
artists.story:
Jean-Michel Basquiat was born in Brooklyn in 1960 (Britannica). In the late 1970s he wrote the SAMO© tags that appeared around downtown Manhattan with Al Diaz (Whitney Museum); Britannica also names Shannon Dawson (Britannica). His first exhibition was The Times Square Show in 1980 (Britannica).

The move from walls to galleries was fast. In 1982 he had solo shows in New York and Los Angeles and was in Documenta 7 in Kassel (Museum of Fine Arts, Boston). He met Andy Warhol in 1983, and the two later painted together (Britannica). He died in New York in 1988, aged 27 (Britannica).
artists.method:
By 1980 he was painting on canvas, drawing crowns, halos and parts of the body in oilstick (Whitney Museum). He also painted on things he found: the Whitney thinks the wooden crossbars in LNAPRK (1982) may have come from the street, and the crown in its lower corner is his old graffiti signature (Whitney Museum).

Words fill the pictures, and many are crossed out. Our reading: that habit comes straight from the wall, where writing over a word is part of how a surface builds up.

works.m: Acrylic, oil, oilstick and marker on found paper on canvas and wood, with rope
works.note: Named after an amusement park outside Milan. Whitney Museum of American Art (Whitney).

works.m: Acrylic and oil stick on canvas
works.note: Painted in Los Angeles. The Whitney identifies the figures as Basquiat with the artists Rammellzee and Toxic, who both came out of graffiti (Whitney).

works.t: Untitled (Leonardo and His Five Grotesque Heads)
works.note: Sold at Christie's New York on 19 November 2026 for US$32.8 million with fees, as reported by The Art Newspaper (The Art Newspaper).

quotes.q: “I cross out words so you will see them more.”
quotes.who: Jean-Michel Basquiat, quoted by the Whitney Museum

OSGEMEOS.alt: A long, brightly coloured mural of yellow-skinned figures in patterned clothes, a giant sleeping face, floating trees and railway tracks running across an orange desert under a purple sky.
OSGEMEOS.caption: Mural by OSGEMEOS at the entrance to the Museu de Arte Moderna in Ibirapuera Park, São Paulo, photographed in March 2011.
OSGEMEOS.credit: Photo: André Deak for Arte Fora do Museu, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

Faith XLVII.alt: A tall painted figure in a dark hooded robe, face lifted and lit from one side, fills the pale green end wall of a block of flats. Bare trees stand in front and ivy climbs the brick beside it.
Faith XLVII.caption: Mural by Faith XLVII on the end wall of a block of flats in Cologne, photographed in February 2015.
Faith XLVII.credit: Photo: Raimond Spekking, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

Konn Artiss.alt: Four performers in black, seen from behind on the Venice waterfront, spell out KONN in white letters across their backs. Two hold umbrellas reading TRUST and ME. Beside them a life-size seated figure reads a newspaper, with San Giorgio Maggiore across the water.
Konn Artiss.caption: Konn Artiss in Venice.

KAWS.alt: KAWS stands in a white-walled room with his hands over his face, among four life-size COMPANION figures with crossed-out eyes, two black and two grey, two of them shown half cut away to reveal their insides.
KAWS.caption: KAWS with four of his COMPANION figures.

Keith Haring.alt: Black and white photograph of Keith Haring, a young man with short hair and round glasses, at work on a large painted surface.
Keith Haring.caption: Keith Haring at the Stedelijk Museum, Amsterdam, 14 March 1986.
Keith Haring.credit: Photo: Rob Bogaerts, Anefo, Nationaal Archief, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons.

Jean-Michel Basquiat.alt: Jean-Michel Basquiat in 1984, a young man with short dreadlocks, photographed indoors.
Jean-Michel Basquiat.caption: Jean-Michel Basquiat, 15 September 1984.
Jean-Michel Basquiat.credit: Photo: Galerie Bruno Bischofberger, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

Ben Eine.alt: A shop shutter at a market painted with a large orange capital D, striped by the shutter’s slats, with a turquoise shadow on its right side.
Ben Eine.caption: A letter D by Ben Eine on a shutter at the Naschmarkt, Vienna, photographed in February 2014.
Ben Eine.credit: Photo: Ungry Young Man, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

JR.alt: JR in a black hat, dark glasses, checked shirt and blue jacket, photographed indoors in 2011.
JR.caption: JR in March 2011, the year he won the TED Prize.
JR.credit: Photo: Mohamed Nanabhay, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons.
